name: Victor Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 58, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I used to sort furniture-warehouse orders, and I'm still less skilled and slower at electrical work than the experienced crew. Today I prepared materials and helped fit parts under supervision; the senior worker had to show me again how the drawing matched the room. I can count fittings in a box better than I can follow a wiring diagram, and I like the moment the second explanation finally makes sense.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I know about life around the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner packs orders in a food shop, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we still have a mortgage. I earn typical trade pay, we've got two months of expenses saved and some other electrical firms nearby, but a heating repair has been quoted at nearly three weeks of expenses. I never use AI tools and prefer the paper drawing and a person I trust showing me the method. Retirement is on my mind, but I haven't verified our old employment records or what income they might provide, if anything. I favour work, proper apprenticeships and family helping family, without assuming somebody else automatically pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quieter future would suit me. The office could improve an invoice without making every familiar method a bad habit. I'd keep asking for the check I needed and try to get the ordinary work right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the heating bill eating into two months of savings. The usual wage covers the usual bills, but it doesn't make that repair a small matter. A quiet AI story doesn't mend the heating or refill the account afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd pause the paid film subscription and use the monthly cost towards ordinary bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep the supervised preparation and fitting work with my paper notes. I'd put the actual heating invoice beside our wages before agreeing to another spending commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household money, with relief that the work itself stays familiar. I'd be glad not to have another new system to learn immediately. I'd still look twice before saying yes to an extra bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about the heating bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's only the quoted cost, and I'd check the actual invoice and what work it covered before paying. I wouldn't pretend every penny of the reserve was spare before that was settled. I'd use the real figure in the budget, not a reassuring guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would replace the film subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the films we already owned and stop the subscription charge. It isn't a second wage or a pension contribution. I'd rather call it a small cut than tell my partner we'd solved the whole future.

fieldNote: His **job search** uses actual applications and former stores experience, rather than promoting him above junior electrical skill or promising permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster office should still leave time to show a beginner the job. I'd ask what paid instruction came with any required new procedure. A neat schedule won't make my hands learn at the speed of a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if the firm allowed less time for a slower beginner while the senior workers got through more planning. I'd have little enthusiasm for losing paid time just as the heating bill landed. My old stores experience might give me another familiar application route, but it wouldn't make a job safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the film subscription paused and inspect actual posted stores-assistant jobs, sorting and handing out materials. In the first year I'd apply only where duties fitted my actual ability, keeping the current wage meanwhile. I'd leave only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essential bills after travel, asking about paid instruction before accepting any unfamiliar required process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours and household money, but able to look at a real advert and ask about the work. I wouldn't enjoy another screen being presented as a test of my attitude. I'd prefer a familiar task with the terms plainly written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would stores work escape the same changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, stock records and customer questions could face thinking AI too, and robots could reach the physical stores work later. I'd want an actual paid opportunity, not a story that an old title kept machines out. I wouldn't leave a paid electrical job to prove an old stores title was safe from machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the vacancy required unfamiliar software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to show me during paid time what it required, keeping the normal pay and hours. I wouldn't claim I could use a system I hadn't learned. If the task didn't fit what I could do or get properly taught, I wouldn't accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 when I'd be 60, with capable robots around 2031 when I'd be 63. I'd still ask what paid work the firm actually planned. Being nearly at a retirement age in someone's imagination wouldn't put an income in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large loss of my junior hours as firms prepared for capable hands-on robots. My partner's physical shop work could change too, and the heating repair would already have reduced our small reserve. I'd be awake wondering what income we really had after the wage, instead of assuming an old employment letter meant a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my son whether he had time to help obtain official retirement information and find available free community advice, without assuming money or an appointment. During 2029 I'd apply for posted stores work only where duties fitted actual ability. I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and leave only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essential bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large wage loss, though still able to sort papers and apply for actual work. I'd want the facts without somebody promising I could just retire. Retirement needs an income figure I can read, not a birthday I can remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask an adviser about the records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what was actually payable, when and on what conditions, and what information was still missing. If support was suggested, I'd check eligibility, whether it was a payment or loan and any later costs. I wouldn't spend an application or an estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your son be agreeing to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be helping find and understand records if he chose, not taking over our mortgage. He has his own household. I'd want to know our actual gap before asking anyone about specific help, and count no family contribution without agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check real work and resources, not assume everybody older has already paid for an exit. I'd be 63 at the thinking change in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still favour proper paid teaching for the actual tasks I had now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have more time to learn the supervised work and check the official retirement records. But today's heating bill and two-month reserve still make me cautious about money. I don't know a confirmed income or suitable future job that automatically begins at 63 or 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my son for record help if he had time and keep suitable supervised work while available. During 2032 we'd compare verified income with essentials and my actual work capacity; if I still needed wages, I'd apply to posted stores roles with suitable duties. I'd leave the current paid job only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essentials after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current money, with less hurry to take the first offered answer. I'd welcome time to check the actual work before changing. I wouldn't count another three years as another agreed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about stores duties at those ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about the actual lifting, standing and required procedures rather than assume old warehouse experience meant I could do every version at any age. I'd need paid teaching with normal pay and hours retained for an unfamiliar compulsory process. I wouldn't accept a job that didn't meet those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income records were incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the provider or former employer what official information could be obtained and keep the budget on confirmed income meanwhile. I wouldn't put a guessed pension amount in to make the figures balance. I'd ask family to help understand the papers before asking about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to find actual figures before telling every older worker they're retired. I'd be 68 at the thinking change in 2036 and about 71 when capable robots followed around 2039. I'd still want a paid day and a person explaining unfamiliar tasks while I needed work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might hope to have stopped by then, but I don't have verified income or costs to say we could afford it. I also can't assume physical capacity, a suitable vacancy or an employer willing to hire me at 68. The present heating repair and two-month reserve still leave me worried today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised work only while available and ask my son about help obtaining official records, without assuming his time or money. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed income, essential costs, actual capacity and suitable work before any exit decision. If I still needed wages, I'd apply only to suitable posted stores work and change only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essentials after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current household account, though less hurried by the far robot date. I'd like enough time to make a plain decision from real figures. I wouldn't write a retirement income into the budget because 68 sounded old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count from your family by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count only help actually chosen and agreed, not wages I imagined because the children were grown. My partner's ability to keep working wouldn't be guaranteed either. We'd need the actual household situation then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a suitable job required a new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for instruction by a person inside paid hours, with normal pay and hours retained, before accepting an unfamiliar compulsory process. I wouldn't claim I'd become an AI user because the date moved. I want to know the job I actually agree to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large junior-wage loss before I've checked what dependable income comes next. Actual paid apprenticeships and help finding the official records would help more than an invitation to buy a course myself. I'd like to read the income before somebody tells me the working years are over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the older worker is experienced at this particular job. I have a vocational certificate and still need the senior worker checking what I do. I'd rather say that plainly than let my age write a qualification I haven't earned.

headlineQuote: I'd like to read the income before somebody tells me the working years are over.
portrait: **Victor, 58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and supervised preparation and fitting work.
His **household** has a partner, grown children, a mortgage, typical trade pay and two months saved, with a substantial heating quote pending.
He **never uses AI**, prefers familiar paid teaching and checks any stores-role application against actual duties, signed pay and travel costs.
Fast change brings **alarm** over expected wage loss; longer horizons don't guarantee retirement resources, children's payments, physical capacity or a future job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because he expects a large junior-wage loss before verifying replacement income.
whatWouldHelp: Actual **paid apprenticeships** would support practical learning without an unaffordable private course bill.
Help obtaining **official income records** would clarify resources without assuming entitlement, payment or future work capacity.
